message.content: {"passages":[{"reference":"12.26","text":"And I answered, “Does it not seem to you, then, that even the innkeeper is humane, since she did good to a woman who was a stranger and whom she did not know?” Peter said, “I know that I can call her merciful, but I do not dare call her humane, since I would not even call a mother child-loving; for she has been persuaded by labor pains and upbringing to cherish her child. Just as the lover is flattered by familiarity and by the bed, and the friend by reciprocation, so also the person who shows mercy is flattered by misfortune. Nevertheless, the merciful person is close to the humane person, because he is persuaded to do good without hunting to receive anything. At least in this way he is humane.” And I said, “By what actions, then, can someone be humane?” Peter answered, “Since I see that you are eager to hear what an act of humaneness actually is, I will not hesitate to tell you. The humane person is one who does good even to enemies. Hear why this is so. Humaneness is male-and-female: its female part is called mercy, while its male part has been named love toward one’s neighbor. Every human being is a human being’s neighbor, not merely some particular human being; for the evil person and the good person, the enemy and the friend, are all human beings. Therefore, the person who practices humaneness must be an imitator of God, doing good to the righteous and the unrighteous, just as God himself provides everyone in the present world with both his sun and his rains. But if you wish to do good to good people, but no longer to evil people, or even to punish them, you are attempting to perform the work of a judge; you are not striving to possess the work of humaneness.”","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"φιλάνθρωπος","chosen":"humane","rationale":"The term denotes active benevolence toward human beings. “Humane” maintains its connection with the recurring noun rendered “humaneness” without narrowing it to institutional philanthropy."},{"source_quote":"οὔτε τὴν τεκοῦσαν φιλότεκνον","chosen":"I would not even call a mother child-loving","rationale":"The verb “call” is carried forward from εἰπεῖν and λέγειν. More literally, τὴν τεκοῦσαν is “the woman who gave birth.”"},{"source_quote":"ὡς καὶ ὁ ἐρῶν ὑπὸ τῆς συνηθείας κολακεύεται καὶ εὐνῆς καὶ ὁ φίλος ὑπὸ τῆς ἀμοιβῆς: οὕτω καὶ ὁ ἐλεῶν ὑπὸ τῆς συμφορᾶς.","chosen":"Just as the lover is flattered by familiarity and by the bed, and the friend by reciprocation, so also the person who shows mercy is flattered by misfortune.","rationale":"The predicate κολακεύεται is understood elliptically in all three members of the analogy. Its unusual image of being flattered or enticed is therefore retained throughout rather than weakened in the final member."},{"source_quote":"ἄνευ τοῦ τι θηρᾶσθαι λαβεῖν","chosen":"without hunting to receive anything","rationale":"The rendering preserves the source’s hunting image and the idea of seeking some return."},{"source_quote":"φιλανθρωπία ἐστὶν ἀρρενόθηλυς","chosen":"Humaneness is male-and-female","rationale":"The compound ἀρρενόθηλυς explicitly combines male and female. The striking image is preserved rather than reduced to “twofold”; “androgynous” would be another possible rendering."},{"source_quote":"τὸ θῆλυ μέρος ἐλεημοσύνη λέγεται","chosen":"its female part is called mercy","rationale":"In this context ἐλεημοσύνη continues the discussion of showing mercy. “Almsgiving” is possible in other contexts but would be too narrow here."},{"source_quote":"πλησίον δὲ ἀνθρώπῳ ἐστὶν ὁ πᾶς ἄνθρωπος, οὐχ ὁ τὶς ἄνθρωπος","chosen":"Every human being is a human being’s neighbor, not merely some particular human being","rationale":"The rendering preserves the contrast between every human being and a neighbor restricted to some particular person."},{"source_quote":"κριτοῦ τὸ ἔργον ἐπιχειρεῖς πράττειν, οὐ τὸ τῆς φιλανθρωπίας σπουδάζεις ἔχειν.","chosen":"you are attempting to perform the work of a judge; you are not striving to possess the work of humaneness","rationale":"The second τὸ is taken elliptically with ἔργον carried forward, preserving the parallel between a judge’s work and the work of humaneness. It could more generally mean “what belongs to humaneness,” including the quality itself."}],"source_issues":[]},{"reference":"12.27","text":"And I said, “Surely God too, since he is going to judge then, as you teach us, is not humane?” Peter replied, “You are saying the opposite. For it is precisely because he will judge that he is humane. In loving and showing mercy to those who have been wronged, he punishes those who wronged them.” And I said, “Therefore, if I too do good to good people but punish those who commit injustice insofar as they have wronged human beings, am I humane?” Peter answered, “If, along with possessing foreknowledge, you also possessed authority to judge, you would rightly do this: on account of having received the authority, you would condemn those whom God created; and because of your foreknowledge, you would judge without error, acquitting some as righteous and condemning others as unrighteous.” And I said, “You have spoken correctly and truthfully, for it is impossible for someone who lacks foreknowledge to judge correctly. Sometimes some people appear good while secretly committing unlawful acts, while some good people are considered evil because of their enemies’ slander. But even if someone possesses authority to torture and interrogate and then judges, it would not even so be possible for him to judge justly in every case. For some who were murderers endured the tortures and were released as innocent, while others who were innocent did not endure the tortures, falsely testified against themselves as guilty, and were punished.”","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"Τοὐναντίον λέγεις","chosen":"You are saying the opposite","rationale":"The expression directly reverses Clement’s inference and does not require an expanded theological explanation."},{"source_quote":"καθὸ ἀνθρώπους ἠδίκησαν","chosen":"insofar as they have wronged human beings","rationale":"ἀνθρώπους is read as the object of ἠδίκησαν, while καθό marks the respect or extent in which punishment is contemplated. Another possible rendering is “because they wronged human beings.”"},{"source_quote":"διὰ μὲν τὸ εἰληφέναι τὴν ἐξουσίαν καταδικάζων οὓς ὁ θεὸς ἐδημιούργησεν","chosen":"on account of having received the authority, you would condemn those whom God created","rationale":"The participle καταδικάζων describes the exercise of the hypothetical authority. The striking reference to condemning people created by God is retained."},{"source_quote":"οὓς μὲν ὡς δικαίους δικαιῶν","chosen":"acquitting some as righteous","rationale":"In this judicial context δικαιόω denotes declaring righteous or acquitting rather than making someone morally righteous."},{"source_quote":"ἐνίοτε γὰρ φαίνονταί τινες ἀγαθοί, ἀθέμιτα κρύφα διαπρασσόμενοι, ἔνιοι δὲ ἀγαθοὶ ὑπὸ διαβολῆς ἐχθρῶν κακοὶ ὑπολαμβανόμενοι.","chosen":"Sometimes some people appear good while secretly committing unlawful acts, while some good people are considered evil because of their enemies’ slander.","rationale":"The first ἐνίοτε is temporal, “sometimes,” but the second expression is ἔνιοι, “some people.” The translation therefore contrasts two groups rather than introducing an unsupported second temporal category."},{"source_quote":"οὐδὲ οὕτως τὸ πάντως δικαίως αὐτῷ δικάσαι ἐγίνετο","chosen":"it would not even so be possible for him to judge justly in every case","rationale":"πάντως is understood distributively in light of the contrasting examples that follow. “To judge altogether justly” is also possible."},{"source_quote":"ἑαυτῶν καταψευσάμενοι ὡς αἴτιοι","chosen":"falsely testified against themselves as guilty","rationale":"The reflexive construction denotes making a false accusation or testimony against oneself, while αἴτιοι denotes culpability or guilt."}],"source_issues":[]},{"reference":"12.28","text":"And Peter said, “These points too are moderately sound, but hear the greater point. When some people sin or act well, among the things they now do some are their own and others belong to someone else; yet it is just for each person to be punished for his own sins or benefited for his own right actions. But it is impossible for anyone except a prophet alone, who possesses foreknowledge, to know which of the things done by someone are his own and which were not his own; for everything is seen to happen through him.” And I said, “I would like to learn how, among acts of injustice or right actions, some are one’s own and others belong to someone else.”","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"Μετρίως, ἔφη, ἔχει καὶ ταῦτα","chosen":"These points too are moderately sound","rationale":"μετρίως gives qualified approval rather than complete endorsement. “These things too are reasonable to a degree” is another possible rendering."},{"source_quote":"ἃ μὲν ἴδια αὐτῶν ἐστίν, ἃ δὲ ἀλλότρια","chosen":"some are their own and others belong to someone else","rationale":"ἴδια and ἀλλότρια contrast actions attributable to the person with actions whose agency or ownership belongs elsewhere."},{"source_quote":"ἐπὶ τοῖς ἰδίοις κατορθώμασιν εὐεργετεῖσθαι","chosen":"benefited for his own right actions","rationale":"κατόρθωμα denotes a right, successful, or virtuous action. “Achievement” is possible but could obscure the moral contrast with sins."},{"source_quote":"πλὴν προφήτῃ μόνῳ πρόγνωσιν ἔχοντι","chosen":"except a prophet alone, who possesses foreknowledge","rationale":"Both the exception marked by πλήν and the exclusivity expressed by μόνῳ are retained."},{"source_quote":"ποῖά, ἐστιν αὐτοῦ ἴδια, ποῖα δὲ οὐχ ἦν","chosen":"which ... are his own and which were not his own","rationale":"The rendering preserves the supplied shift from present ἐστιν to past ἦν while supplying “his own” in the second member from the first. Regularizing ἦν to a present tense would require emendation."},{"source_quote":"πάντα γὰρ δι’ αὐτοῦ γινόμενα βλέπεται","chosen":"for everything is seen to happen through him","rationale":"The participial phrase is taken predicatively with βλέπεται: all the actions appear to occur through the person, even though only a prophet can discern which are truly the person’s own. It could also be construed as “everything that happens through him is seen.”"}],"source_issues":[{"source_quote":"ποῖά, ἐστιν αὐτοῦ ἴδια, ποῖα δὲ οὐχ ἦν","issue":"The printed comma after ποῖά is editorially awkward, and the shift from present ἐστιν to past ἦν is abrupt. The supplied wording nevertheless permits a defensible translation without changing the Greek.","proposed_reading":"","blocks_publication":false}]},{"reference":"12.29","text":"And Peter answered, “The prophet of truth said, ‘The good things must come; but blessed (he says) is the one through whom they come. Likewise, the evil things must necessarily come; but woe to the one through whom they come.’ Now if evil things come through evil people and good things are borne through good people, what is each person’s own—being good or evil—must also belong to him on the basis of the things he did beforehand, through the coming of the subsequent good or evil things. These, being his own as matters of choice, have been arranged by God’s providence to pass through him. God’s judgment, then, is this: just as in a contest, the one who has passed through every hardship and been found blameless is to be deemed worthy of eternal life. For those who, by their own resolve, have come to the fore in good things are tested by those who, by their own resolve, have persisted in evil: they are persecuted, hated, reviled, plotted against, beaten, exploited, slandered, pressed into service, and abused, suffering all those things through which becoming angry and rushing toward retaliation seem reasonably to arise.”","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"τὰ ἀγαθὰ ἐλθεῖν δεῖ, μακάριος δὲ (φησίν) δι’ οὗ ἔρχεται","chosen":"The good things must come; but blessed (he says) is the one through whom they come","rationale":"The positive form of the saying is translated as supplied rather than harmonized with a familiar parallel, and the separate parenthetical attribution φησίν is explicitly retained."},{"source_quote":"τὰ κακὰ ἀνάγκη ἐλθεῖν, οὐαὶ δὲ δι’ οὗ ἔρχεται","chosen":"the evil things must necessarily come; but woe to the one through whom they come","rationale":"ἀνάγκη expresses necessity. The singular Greek verb treats the neuter plural collectively, while idiomatic English uses a plural verb."},{"source_quote":"προσεῖναι δεῖ ἑκάστῳ τὸ ἴδιον (τὸ ἀγαθὸν εἶναι ἢ κακόν) καὶ ἐξ ὧν προέπραξεν","chosen":"what is each person’s own—being good or evil—must also belong to him on the basis of the things he did beforehand","rationale":"The parenthesis identifies what is proper to the person as being good or evil. The compressed καὶ ἐξ ὧν προέπραξεν is taken as identifying the basis supplied by prior conduct; it could alternatively mean that the person’s character is known from what he previously did."},{"source_quote":"ἅτινα ἴδια αὐτοῦ τῆς αἱρέσεως ὄντα","chosen":"These, being his own as matters of choice","rationale":"αἵρεσις is understood as personal choice or resolve. The compact genitive construction could also be represented as “belonging to his own choice.”"},{"source_quote":"ὑπὸ τῆς τοῦ θεοῦ προνοίας διελθεῖν ᾠκονόμηται","chosen":"have been arranged by God’s providence to pass through him","rationale":"The subject is the preceding good or evil things. “Through him” is contextually supplied from the repeated description of events coming through good or evil agents; a less agent-focused alternative is “have been arranged by God’s providence to run their course.”"},{"source_quote":"ἐπεὶ οὖν κρίσις αὕτη θεῷ","chosen":"God’s judgment, then, is this","rationale":"The compressed nominal clause introduces the content expressed by the following accusative-and-infinitive construction. More formally, it could be rendered “For this, then, is judgment with God” or “Since this judgment belongs to God.”"},{"source_quote":"οἱ γὰρ ἐν ἀγαθοῖς ἰδίᾳ βουλῇ προκύψαντες","chosen":"For those who, by their own resolve, have come to the fore in good things","rationale":"The rendering follows the supplied προκύψαντες from προκύπτω, conveying emergence or coming forward. It does not silently substitute προκόψαντες, which would more directly mean “advanced” or “made progress.”"},{"source_quote":"ἀγγαρευόμενοι","chosen":"pressed into service","rationale":"The verb denotes being compelled to perform service or labor, so the coercive force is retained."},{"source_quote":"πρὸς ἄμυναν ὁρμᾶν","chosen":"rushing toward retaliation","rationale":"ἄμυνα can denote defense or retaliatory action. “Retaliation” fits the following warning against responding to mistreatment in kind, though “self-defense” remains possible."}],"source_issues":[{"source_quote":"οἱ γὰρ ἐν ἀγαθοῖς ἰδίᾳ βουλῇ προκύψαντες;","issue":"The printed Greek semicolon functions as a question mark, but the clause continues syntactically with ὑπὸ τῶν ... πειράζονται and is defensibly read as declarative. The punctuation is treated provisionally as an editorial oddity, not as evidence that wording is missing.","proposed_reading":"οἱ γὰρ ἐν ἀγαθοῖς ἰδίᾳ βουλῇ προκύψαντες,","blocks_publication":false},{"source_quote":"ἐπεὶ οὖν κρίσις αὕτη θεῷ, ὥσπερ ἐπ᾽ ἀγῶνος τὸν διὰ πάσης κακουχίας διεληλυθότα καὶ ἄμεμπτον εὑρεθέντα, ἐκεῖνον ζωῆς αἰωνίου καταξιοῦσθαι —·","issue":"The construction is compressed, with a nominal statement followed by an accusative-and-infinitive formulation, and the closing dash and point are editorially unusual. The translation treats the infinitive as defining the stated judgment; this is provisional but defensible without restoring, deleting, or altering words.","proposed_reading":"","blocks_publication":false}]},{"reference":"12.30","text":"“But the Teacher, knowing that those who do these things unjustly stand condemned because of earlier sins, and that through condemned people the spirit of evil carries out these things, counseled them, as people practicing humaneness, to have mercy on human beings insofar as they are human, even though through sin they become instruments of evil. He also counseled them, as far as it lay with them, while being wronged, to release the wrongdoers from condemnation, so that, just as sober people help drunk people, they might help them with prayers, fasts, and blessings, neither resisting nor retaliating, so that they would not force them to sin still more. For when suffering has in any event been decreed for someone, it is not reasonable for that person to be indignant with the one through whom the suffering comes, when he reflects that even if that person had not mistreated him, because he was in any event going to be mistreated, the suffering would have come through someone else. Why, then, am I indignant with the one who brought it about, when it has in any event been decreed that I suffer? But moreover, if on the pretext of retaliation we do the same things as evil people, then, apart from being second rather than first, we who are good do the same thing as evil people. And (as I said) one should not be indignant, knowing that by God’s providence evil people punish good people. Those, therefore, who are angry with those who punish them sin as people who insult God’s emissaries; but those who honor them and treat them with the opposite of what is considered injurious act reverently toward God, who has so resolved.”","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"διὰ καταδίκων τὸ τῆς κακίας πνεῦμα ταῦτα ἐνεργεῖ","chosen":"through condemned people the spirit of evil carries out these things","rationale":"The condemned people are represented as intermediate agents through whom the spirit acts. The author’s claim is retained without theological harmonization."},{"source_quote":"τοὺς μὲν ἀνθρώπους καθὰ ἄνθρωποί εἰσιν, καὶ δι᾽ ἁμαρτίας ὄργανα γινομένους κακίας ἐλεεῖν συνεβούλευσεν, ὡς φιλανθρωπίαν ἀσκοῦσιν","chosen":"counseled them, as people practicing humaneness, to have mercy on human beings insofar as they are human, even though through sin they become instruments of evil","rationale":"ἀσκοῦσιν is read as a dative plural participle referring to the implicitly counseled hearers. κακίας is taken with ὄργανα, while δι᾽ ἁμαρτίας identifies how people become such instruments. The concessive “even though” expresses the contrast between their humanity and their instrumental role."},{"source_quote":"τὸ ὅσον ἐπ᾽ αὐτοῖς ἐστίν","chosen":"as far as it lay with them","rationale":"The idiom limits the action to what lies within their power. “As far as depended on them” is a more literal alternative."},{"source_quote":"ὥσπερ οἱ νήφοντες τοῖς μεθύουσιν βοηθῶσιν","chosen":"just as sober people help drunk people","rationale":"Because νήφοντες is explicitly contrasted with μεθύουσιν, the literal sober-versus-drunk image is retained rather than generalized to “clear-minded.”"},{"source_quote":"μὴ ἀνθιστάμενοι, μὴ ἀμυνόμενοι","chosen":"neither resisting nor retaliating","rationale":"ἀνθίστημι denotes resistance, while ἀμύνομαι can mean defending oneself or retaliating. The latter sense fits the repeated warning against returning harmful acts, though “nor defending themselves” remains possible."},{"source_quote":"τοῦ γὰρ παθεῖν πάντως κεκριμένου τινί","chosen":"when suffering has in any event been decreed for someone","rationale":"πάντως is understood as expressing inevitability in this argument. The genitive construction supplies the circumstance under which indignation is declared unreasonable."},{"source_quote":"τί οὖν ἀγανακτῶ τῷ διαθεμένῳ","chosen":"Why, then, am I indignant with the one who brought it about","rationale":"διατίθημι is elliptical here and refers to the person who occasioned the suffering. “The one who dealt with me this way” is another possible rendering."},{"source_quote":"εἰ τὰ αὐτὰ τοῖς κακοῖς προφάσει ἀμύνης ποιῶμεν, παρὰ τὸ πρῶτοι δεύτεροι τὸ αὐτὸ τοῖς κακοῖς οἱ ἀγαθοὶ πράσσομεν.","chosen":"if on the pretext of retaliation we do the same things as evil people, then, apart from being second rather than first, we who are good do the same thing as evil people","rationale":"The datives τοῖς κακοῖς are comparative with τὰ αὐτά and τὸ αὐτό: the good do the same things as the evil, rather than doing those things to evil people. The compressed πρῶτοι δεύτεροι contrasts initiating the conduct with repeating it in response."},{"source_quote":"ὡς τοὺς ἀποστόλους θεοῦ ὑβρίζοντες","chosen":"as people who insult God’s emissaries","rationale":"ἀπόστολοι is used generically for people functioning as sent agents, not necessarily for holders of the particular apostolic office. “Messengers” is also possible."},{"source_quote":"τιμῶντες δὲ καὶ τὰ ἐναντία τοῖς ἀδικεῖν νομιζομένοις διατιθέμενοι αὐτοὺς","chosen":"but those who honor them and treat them with the opposite of what is considered injurious","rationale":"τοῖς ... νομιζομένοις is taken as neuter, referring to things considered injurious, which supplies a defensible comparison without adding a customary way in which wrongdoers are treated. A masculine construal is possible—“treating them in ways opposite to those regarded as doing wrong”—but leaves the exact relation of the comparison more compressed."},{"source_quote":"εἰς τὸν θεὸν τὸν οὕτω βουλευσάμενον εὐσεβοῦσιν","chosen":"act reverently toward God, who has so resolved","rationale":"εὐσεβέω denotes reverent or pious conduct toward God. βουλεύομαι is understood as resolving or determining the providential arrangement; “who has planned it this way” is also possible."}],"source_issues":[]}]}
